fire: Sharks detect the faint electric fields of buried prey using electroreceptors called the ampullae of Lorenzini.
Many migratory birds rely on magnetoreception to orient themselves along the Earth's magnetic field lines.
The lateral line running along a fish's flank senses tiny changes in water pressure from nearby movement.
A dragonfly's compound eyes contain tens of thousands of ommatidia, giving it a nearly panoramic field of view.
Bats navigate in total darkness by echolocation, emitting high-pitched calls and listening for the returning echoes.
Pit vipers have heat pits between the eye and nostril that let them strike warm-blooded prey at night.
The platypus bill is lined with mechanoreceptors and electroreceptors that pick up the muscle twitches of shrimp.
Star-nosed moles explore tunnels with a fleshy organ packed with thousands of touch-sensitive Eimer's organs.
quiet: Sharks hunt buried prey along the sandy seabed, often patrolling shallow lagoons at dusk.
Many migratory birds fly thousands of kilometres each autumn to reach their wintering grounds in Africa.
The scales running along a fish's flank overlap like roof tiles and protect it from abrasion.
A dragonfly's wings beat independently, letting it hover, dart sideways and even fly backwards.
Bats roost in caves during the day, hanging upside down in clusters that can number in the thousands.
Pit vipers are mostly ambush hunters that wait motionless among leaf litter for passing rodents.
The platypus is one of only a few mammals that lay eggs, incubating them in a burrow for about ten days.
Star-nosed moles dig extensive tunnel systems in wet meadows and are surprisingly good swimmers.
